extracted.intended_audience: judges, patent litigators, and juries in U.S. patent infringement trials
extracted.subtask_description: Model jury instructions for determining patent damages (lost profits, reasonable royalty, related doctrines) and willfulness in U.S. patent litigation. Provides legal standards, evidentiary burdens, enumerated factors, and practical notes for juries and trial counsel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice by Marking (public notice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Public notice by marking: marking substantially all products with 'Patent' or 'Pat' and a freely accessible Internet address that connects the product with the patent number(s). Licensees who use the invention must also mark substantially all their products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This form of public notice starts from the date the plaintiff (and its licensees) began marking substantially all products that use the invention. If the plaintiff (and licensees) did not mark substantially all such products, then the plaintiff did not provide notice in this way. Notice to the public via marking is effective even if the defendant did not see or was not aware of the notice to the public. Relevant statutes and cases: 35 U.S.C. §§ 286, 287(a); Arctic Cat v. Bombardier; Funai v. Daewoo; etc. Practice note: If the plaintiff and any licensees never made, offered for sale, or sold any patented products (or only method claims are asserted), the plaintiff can recover damages up to six years before suit even without giving notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct Notice to Defendant
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct notice: the plaintiff can give notice by directly notifying the defendant with a specific claim that the allegedly infringing product infringed the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This type of notice begins on the date the defendant received the notice. If plaintiff provided neither effective public marking nor direct notice before filing suit, plaintiff can only recover damages for infringement that occurred after it sued the defendant (the suit filing date).

rubrics_metrics.name: Kinds of Damages Available
rubrics_metrics.description: There are several kinds of damages available for patent infringement, primarily lost profits and reasonable royalty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lost profits measure additional profits the patentee would have made 'but for' the infringement. A reasonable royalty is the amount a willing licensee would have paid the patent owner just before infringement began, and is the minimum recovery if lost profits are not awarded. (Cites: 35 U.S.C. § 284; Rude v. Westcott; Lucent v. Gateway, etc.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Lost Profits — 'But For' Test
rubrics_metrics.description: To obtain lost-profits damages, the plaintiff must show that, but for the defendant’s infringement, the plaintiff would have made additional profits through the sale of all or a portion of the infringing sales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plaintiff must prove lost profits by a preponderance of the evidence. Jurors must determine what purchasers would have done absent infringement. The profits at issue are the profits allegedly lost by plaintiff, not profits made by defendant. (Cites: Am. Seating Co.; Aro Mfg.; Ericsson; Tate Access Floors.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Panduit Factor — Demand for the Patented Product/Method
rubrics_metrics.description: One Panduit factor: a demand for the patented product or method in the relevant market.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plaintiff can prove demand by showing significant sales of its own patented product/method or demand for a product/method that directly competes with the defendant’s infringing product/method. Plaintiff may also rely on significant sales of the defendant’s product covered by the asserted claims, but only if the plaintiff’s and defendant’s products are sufficiently similar to compete in the same market or segment. (Cites: DePuy Spine; BIC Leisure.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Panduit Factor — Absence of Acceptable Non-Infringing Substitutes
rubrics_metrics.description: Second Panduit factor: absence of acceptable non-infringing substitutes that competed with the infringing product/method in the marketplace and their impact absent the defendant’s sales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An acceptable substitute must have one or more advantages of the patented invention important to actual buyers (not the public at large), must be non-infringing (either licensed or lacking one or more claimed features), and must have been available during the damages period (need not have actually been sold). If a substitute was not sold during the damages period, the defendant must show by preponderance that a competitor had the equipment, materials, know-how, and experience to design and make the substitute. If some customers would likely have bought substitutes, plaintiff is not entitled to lost profits for those sales. Even if only plaintiff and defendant had the patented advantages, plaintiff still must prove it would have made the defendant’s sales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panduit Factor — Market Share (portion of infringing sales)
rubrics_metrics.description: If acceptable non-infringing substitutes existed, plaintiff may still recover lost profits for a portion of defendant’s sales equal to plaintiff’s market share.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plaintiff bears the burden to prove by a preponderance that it competed in the same market and would have made at least a portion of the infringing sales equal to its market share. It is not necessary to prove the plaintiff and defendant were the only suppliers. (Cites: DePuy Spine; Ericsson; Crystal Semiconductor; BIC Leisure; State Indus.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Panduit Factor — Capacity (manufacturing and marketing ability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Third Panduit factor: plaintiff had the manufacturing and marketing ability to make all or part of the infringing sales actually made by defendant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plaintiff must prove it could have supplied the additional products or that someone working with plaintiff could have supplied them, and that it more likely than not had the ability to market and sell these additional products. (Cites: Wechsler v. Macke; Fonar v. GE; Datascope; Gyromat.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Panduit Factor — Amount of Profit (incremental income approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fourth Panduit factor: the amount of profit plaintiff would have made if not for defendant’s infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plaintiff may calculate lost profits by estimating lost sales and subtracting additional costs plaintiff would have incurred to make those sales. The amount cannot be speculative but need not be proven with unerring certainty. (Cites: Kalman; King Instrument; Paper Converting; Bio-Rad; Lam.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Price Erosion Damages
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaintiff may recover additional damages for price erosion if it proves that, but for defendant’s infringement, plaintiff would have been able to charge higher prices or would not have had to lower prices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Award may equal the difference between profits at the higher price and actual profits at the lower price. If price erosion is found, the higher price may be used in determining plaintiff’s lost sales and lost profits, but any decrease in sales due to the higher price must also be taken into account. (Cites: Siemens Med. Sols.; Ericsson; Vulcan Eng'g; Rite-Hite; BIC Leisure; Lam.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost Escalation
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaintiff can recover additional damages for increased costs (e.g., marketing costs) that it incurred because of defendant’s infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plaintiff must prove by a preponderance that its costs increased because of defendant’s actions and not for some other reason. (Cites: Amstar Corp.; Lam.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Convoyed Sales (collateral products)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaintiff may seek damages for lost sales of collateral (convoyed) products ordinarily sold along with the patented product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To recover lost profits for collateral products, plaintiff must prove (1) it is more likely than not that it would have sold the collateral products but for the infringement, and (2) the collateral products and the patented product/method are so closely related that they effectively act or are used together for a common purpose. Damages for lost collateral sales are calculated the same way as for lost profits on the patented product/method. (Cites: DePuy Spine; Rite-Hite; State Indus.; Paper Converting.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable Royalty — General Principle
rubrics_metrics.description: A reasonable royalty is the minimum amount of damages the patent owner can receive for infringement and must be enough to compensate for the infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A reasonable royalty should be based on the incremental value that the patented invention adds to the end product; where accused products have both patented and unpatented features, the royalty must reflect only the value attributable to the patented features and no more. (Cites: 35 U.S.C. § 284; Power Integrations; Exmark; Ericsson v. D-Link; VirnetX; Apple v. Motorola; Uniloc; Lucent.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable Royalty — Hypothetical Negotiation Method (definition and assumptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the hypothetical negotiation method, a reasonable royalty is the royalty that would have resulted from a hypothetical license negotiation between the plaintiff and the defendant just before infringement began.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For the hypothetical negotiation, assume the parties would have negotiated a license, that both understood the patent was valid and infringed, were willing to license, and had full knowledge of facts and circumstances surrounding the infringement at that time. (Cites: Apple v. Motorola; LaserDynamics; Uniloc; Fujifilm; Lucent; Maxwell; Rite-Hite; Wang Labs.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable Royalty — Royalties Received by Licensor (established royalty)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider any royalties previously received by the licensor for licensing the patent-in-suit as evidence of an established royalty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Past licenses for the patent can prove or tend to prove an established royalty rate and are a factor jurors may consider if relevant and supported by admitted evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable Royalty — Comparable Licensing Rates Paid by Defendant
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider rates paid by the defendant to license other patents comparable to the patent-in-suit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence of defendant’s rates for comparable patents can inform the hypothetical negotiation analysis if properly supported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable Royalty — Nature and Scope of the License
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the nature and scope of the license (exclusive vs. non-exclusive; territorial or other restrictions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The terms (exclusive/non-exclusive, territory, restrictions on sales) affect the value and should be considered when estimating a hypothetical royalty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable Royalty — Licensor’s Policy to Preserve Exclusivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the licensor’s established policy and marketing program to maintain its right to exclude others (e.g., not licensing or licensing under special conditions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A licensor’s strategy to preserve exclusivity (or to license only under conditions) can impact the hypothetical royalty outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable Royalty — Commercial Relationship Between Licensor and Licensee
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the commercial relationship between the licensor and licensee, such as whether they are competitors in the same territory and line of business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether parties are competitors, collaborators, or otherwise related commercially affects negotiation dynamics and royalty amounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable Royalty — Effect on Other Sales / Collateral Sales
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the effect of selling the patented product/method in promoting other sales of the licensee and the invention’s value as a generator of sales of non-patented items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The existing value of the invention to the licensor in generating collateral sales and the extent of such sales are relevant to royalty calculation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable Royalty — Patent Duration and License Term
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the duration of the patent and the term of the license.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Length of patent life and license term affect the present value of royalties and negotiation outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable Royalty — Established Profitability, Commercial Success, Popularity
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the established profitability of the product made under the patent, its commercial success, and popularity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commercial success and established profitability are indicators of economic value relevant to a reasonable royalty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable Royalty — Utility and Advantages Over Old Modes
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the utility and advantages of the patented invention over prior modes or devices used for similar results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The technical utility and advantages relative to prior art affect the economic value and bargaining position.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable Royalty — Nature and Commercial Embodiment of the Invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the nature of the patented invention, the character of its commercial embodiment, and the benefits to those who have used the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: How the invention is embodied commercially and the realized benefits to users inform valuation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable Royalty — Extent of Defendant’s Use and Value of Use
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the extent to which the defendant has made use of the invention and any evidence showing the value of that use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Degree and manner of defendant’s exploitation of the invention contribute to royalty assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable Royalty — Customary Portion of Profit or Selling Price
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the portion of profit or selling price that may be customary in the business to allow for the use of the invention or analogous inventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Industry norms for allocating profit or price to the right to use an invention are relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable Royalty — Apportionment: Profit from Patented Feature vs Unpatented Features
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the portion of profit that arises from the patented invention itself as opposed to profit arising from unpatented features, manufacturing process, business risks, or improvements added by the accused infringer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Royalty must reflect only the value attributable to the patented features (apportionment). Cannot base royalty on entire product value without tying value to patented features. (Cites: Power Integrations; Exmark; AstraZeneca; Ericsson; Apple; VirnetX; Versata; Uniloc; ResQNet; Lucent.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable Royalty — Opinion Testimony of Qualified Experts
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider opinion testimony of qualified experts regarding a reasonable royalty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expert economic and licensing testimony is admissible and may inform the jury’s hypothetical negotiation analysis, subject to evidentiary rules and relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable Royalty — Parties’ Hypothetical Agreement (prudent licensee/prudent patentee)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the amount that a licensor and licensee would have agreed upon at the time infringement began if both were reasonably and voluntarily trying to reach agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The jury should consider what a prudent licensee would have been willing to pay while still making reasonable profit and what amount a willing patentee would have accepted. This is the core hypothetical negotiation construct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable Royalty — Any Other Economic Factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider any other economic factor that a normally prudent business person would take into account in negotiating the hypothetical license.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts list this as a catch-all: jurors may consider other relevant economic evidence not specifically enumerated among the factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable Royalty — Attribution/Apportionment (royalty base & rate)
rubrics_metrics.description: Damages must be based on the value attributable to the patented features, distinct from unpatented features or other factors (marketing, defendant’s size, market position).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The royalty base must be closely tied to the invention; it is improper to select a royalty base that is too high and then adjust down via a lower rate, or pick a base too low and adjust up with a higher rate. The ultimate combination of royalty base and rate must reflect value attributable to the patented technology. (Cites: Power Integrations; Exmark; AstraZeneca; Ericsson; Apple; VirnetX; Versata; Uniloc; ResQNet; Lucent.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Entire Market Value Rule (EMVR)
rubrics_metrics.description: General rule: royalties should be based on the smallest salable unit that practices the patented invention and is closely related to the claimed invention; EMVR is a narrow exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the smallest salable unit is a multi-component product with non-infringing components unrelated to the patented feature, damages must be based only on the portion of that unit’s value attributable to the patented technology. The EMVR permits using entire product revenues only if the patentee proves the patented feature is the sole driver of customer demand or substantially creates the product's value. (Cites: Ericsson v. D-Link; VirnetX; LaserDynamics; Uniloc; Lucent; Rite-Hite.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable Royalty — Multiple Patents
rubrics_metrics.description: When multiple patents are infringed by the same act, separate royalties may be awarded for each patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jury may award separate royalties for each infringed patent and may consider evidence on the number of patent licenses needed for the accused product and the effect on the hypothetical negotiation of paying multiple royalties. (Cites: Ericsson; Apple; Verizon; Stickle.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable Royalty — Timing of the Hypothetical Negotiation
rubrics_metrics.description: Damages should be based on what parties to the hypothetical negotiation would have agreed upon at the time just before the infringement began.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not base damages on hindsight; however, parties may consider information they would have foreseen or estimated at negotiation time. Under some circumstances, evidence of usage after infringement began, subsequent licenses, infringer profits, and non-infringing alternatives may be considered if they would have been foreseeable at the negotiation date. (Cites: 35 U.S.C. § 284; Aqua Shield; Lucent; Studiengesellschaft; Sinclair.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable Royalty — Availability and Cost of Non-Infringing Substitutes
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider evidence concerning the availability and cost of acceptable non-infringing substitutes to the patented invention when determining a reasonable royalty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An acceptable substitute must be licensed under the patent or not infringe. Evidence regarding substitutes’ availability and cost is relevant to valuation. (Cites: Prism Techs.; Mars v. Coin Acceptors; Zygo v. Wyko.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable Royalty — Use of Comparable License Agreements
rubrics_metrics.description: When available, consider amounts other parties have paid for rights to the patent-in-suit or comparable technologies as evidence in determining a reasonable royalty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A license need not be perfectly comparable to be considered, but if relied upon, differences between those licenses and the hypothetical license (technologies, economic circumstances) must be accounted for in the reasonable royalty determination. (Cites: Ericsson; Apple; LaserDynamics; ResQNet; Lucent.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Doubts Resolved Against the Infringer (adverse inference for poor records)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any doubts about damages due to the defendant’s failure to keep proper records should be decided in favor of the plaintiff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confusion or difficulties caused by the defendant’s records or lack of records should be held against the defendant, not the plaintiff. (Cites: Bigelow; Story Parchment; Minco; Sensonics; Lam.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard-Essential Patents (SEPs) — FRAND and Apportionment Practice Note
rubrics_metrics.description: For SEPs, the jury must be instructed on the particular FRAND commitment made by the patentee, on established patent law principles, and only those Georgia‑Pacific factors that are relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The jury must not be instructed on irrelevant Georgia‑Pacific factors. The jury must be instructed on apportionment of the value of the portion of the standard as a whole to which the patented technology relates and on apportionment of the value of the claimed invention as opposed to value added by standardization. (Cites: CSIRO v. Cisco; Ericsson v. D-Link; Apple v. Motorola.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Willful Infringement — General Standard
rubrics_metrics.description: To find infringement willful, plaintiff must prove by a preponderance of the evidence that the defendant knew of the plaintiff’s patent and intentionally infringed at least one asserted claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jury may consider whether the defendant’s behavior was deliberate or intentional, but cannot find willfulness solely because the defendant knew about the patent. Consider all circumstances and defendant’s knowledge at the time the conduct occurred. If infringement is willful, that determination should not affect the amount of the damages award. (Cites: Eko Brands; Halo.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Willful Infringement — Reliance on Legal Opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidance on whether reliance on a legal opinion rebuts willfulness and the effect of the AIA amendment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 35 U.S.C. § 298 bars using failure to obtain advice of counsel to prove willfulness. If defendant relies on a lawyer’s opinion that its product did not infringe or that claims were invalid/unenforceable, the jury may consider reasonable reliance on a competent legal opinion as one factor in the totality of circumstances. If defendant does not rely on an opinion, absence of an opinion is not enough to find willfulness; the issue is whether plaintiff proved willfulness considering all circumstances.
